points.point: A-TMA names the failure 'ghost memory': old, current and transition facts coexist in the bank, stay mixed during retrieval and reach the answer model without a state role (a former address should answer 'where did the user live before?' but not 'where should the package ship?'). It argues deletion loses history and timestamps or relevance alone do not expose which fact to use.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/A-TMA. Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory.md
points.evidence: Abstract and §1 (p. 1): 'ghost memory, a state coordination failure in which old, current, and transition facts coexist in the memory bank, remain mixed during retrieval, and mislead the answer model … simple deletion loses history, while timestamps or relevance scores alone do not expose which fact sho[uld be used]'. The former-address example is in §1.

points.point: A-TMA's fix keeps superseded records and labels them active/current, superseded/historical or transition at three levels (bank, retrieval, QA), passing the labels to the answer model and building evidence for the state the query asks about.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/A-TMA. Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory.md
points.evidence: §4.2 (p. 6): three modules for bank state maintenance, state-aligned retrieval and QA with explicit state roles. §4.5 (p. 9) and A.8: the QA prompt prepends each retrieved row with 'current memory, historical memory, transition memory, transition linked memory, or retrieved memory'.

points.point: On the full LTP benchmark, Graphiti/Zep has 0.711 evidence support but only 0.480 conflict accuracy; adding A-TMA raises conflict accuracy to 0.720 (+0.240).
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/A-TMA. Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory.md
points.evidence: Table 2 (p. 10): Graphiti/Zep evidence support 0.711, QA Acc 0.524, conflict 0.480; +A-TMA evidence support 0.809, Acc 0.635, conflict 0.720 (↑0.240). §1: 'improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute, from 0.480 to 0.720'.

points.point: On one LTP profile, temporal-KG (Graphiti/Zep) evidence reaches 0.812 evidence support but only 0.425 conflict accuracy; with A-TMA state roles conflict accuracy rises to 0.725, so timestamps and graph labels alone are not enough.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/A-TMA. Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory.md
points.evidence: §1 (p. 1–2), on LTP profile000: 'Temporal KG evidence reaches 0.812 evidence support but only 0.425 conflict accuracy, while Graphiti/Zep +A-TMA raises conflict accuracy to 0.725 by exposing state roles to QA.' This is a single-profile subset, not the full benchmark.

points.point: A-TMA's evidence is weak or mixed: gains are host- and metric-dependent; on LoCoMo temporal F1 rises only from 0.0295 to 0.1705 (average F1 0.08 to 0.16) while temporal accuracy falls from 0.3707 to 0.3178; the answer model is a 3B model; the component ablation shows small, mixed effects.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/A-TMA. Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory.md
points.evidence: §5.3 (p. 11): 'A-TMA effects are host and metric dependent: Graphiti/Zep +A-TMA raises temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705 and average F1 from 0.0809 to 0.1556 … a mixed generalization check'. Tables 3–4 show 0.3707 for Graphiti/Zep and 0.3178 with A-TMA. §4.5: QA uses qwen2.5:3b. A.10 (p. 20): 'The ablation shows small and mixed component effects', on 3 profiles with an A-Mem host.

points.point: Zep/Graphiti uses a bitemporal model with four timestamps per fact edge (when it was true, when the system learned it). A contradicting new edge invalidates the old one by setting its t_invalid to the new edge's t_valid instead of deleting it, and new information is always prioritised.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Zep. A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory.md
points.evidence: §2.2.3 (p. 3): 'the system tracks four timestamps: t′created and t′expired … while t_valid and t_invalid ∈ T track the temporal range during which facts held true'; 'it invalidates the affected edges by setting their t_invalid to the t_valid of the invalidating edge … Graphiti consistently prioritizes new information'.

points.point: In Zep's own LongMemEval results, knowledge-update accuracy falls with gpt-4o-mini (76.9% to 74.4%) and rises only with gpt-4o (78.2% to 83.3%); the result is vendor-run.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Zep. A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory.md
points.evidence: §4.3.2 table (p. 7): knowledge-update gpt-4o-mini 76.9% → 74.4% (3.36%↓); gpt-4o 78.2% → 83.3% (6.52%↑). The text says 'additional development may be needed to improve less capable models' understanding of Zep's temporal data'.

points.point: Mem0 handles updates at write time: for each extracted fact it retrieves the most similar stored memories (s = 10 in the experiments) and an LLM picks ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP. Its graph variant marks obsolete relations invalid instead of removing them.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Mem0. Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory.md
points.evidence: §2.1 (p. 3–4): 'retrieves the top s semantically similar memories … The LLM itself determines which of four distinct operations to execute'; 's = 10 similar memories'. §2.2 (p. 5): 'marking them as invalid rather than physically removing them to enable temporal reasoning'.

points.point: Memory-R1 trains the ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP choice with RL because the untrained manager misreads complementary facts (two dogs adopted in different sessions) as a contradiction and issues DELETE+ADD.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Memory-R1. Enhancing Large Language Model Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via Reinforcement.md
points.evidence: Figure 1 (p. 1): 'the user mentions adopting two dogs across sessions. (Middle) The vanilla Memory Manager misinterprets this as a contradiction and issues DELETE+ADD, fragmenting memory. (Right) The RL-trained Memory Manager issues a single UPDATE'.

points.point: On LongMemEval knowledge-update questions in an independent comparison, Zep leads with 44.4 Substring EM (Cognee 37.8), while Mem0 (15.6), Letta (17.8) and SimpleMem (6.7) fall below plain long context (20.0).
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System.md
points.evidence: Table 2, §4.3 (p. 9), Knowledge Update Substring EM: Long Context 20.0, Embedding RAG 20.0, Mem0 15.6, Cognee 37.8, Zep 44.4, Letta 17.8, LightMem 15.6, SimpleMem 6.7. Text: 'Zep leads Knowledge Update with 44.4 Substring EM'. The metric is Substring EM, not plain exact match.

points.point: The same study finds graph-organised stores handle knowledge updates most reliably, while fact-extraction plugins and append-only stores return stale facts ('hallucinations of the past'); reliable post-update behaviour is a pipeline design problem, not a model-capacity one; and consolidation destroys chronological cues, so raw long context still wins on time-dependent queries.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System.md
points.evidence: §1 finding ❸: 'Graph-based methods handle knowledge updates most reliably, whereas popular fact-extraction plugins and append-only stores struggle with targeted overwrites. Systems lacking lifecycle management return stale facts, leading to "hallucinations of the past".' Finding ❹: 'standard semantic consolidation often destroys crucial chronological cues'. Finding 3 (p. 9): 'a pipeline-level design problem rather than a pure model-capacity problem'. The study covers 12 systems; Table 2's text says 11.

points.point: On MemoryAgentBench's FactConsolidation (selective forgetting) task, every method scores at most 28% on multi-hop questions over updated facts.
points.paper: llm/memory/benchmarks/Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions.md
points.evidence: §4.2 (p. 8): 'all methods fail on the multi-hop situation (with achieving at most 28% accuracy). Only long context agents can achieve fairly reasonable results on single-hop scenarios.'

points.point: FactConsolidation is built from MQuAKE counterfactual edit pairs with an explicit 'newer facts have larger serial numbers' rule, and still collapses with length: o4-mini scores 100 single-hop and 80 multi-hop at 6K tokens, but 61 and 14 at 32K.
points.paper: llm/memory/benchmarks/Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions.md
points.evidence: §4.3.4, Table 5 (p. 10): O4-mini FactCon-SH 100.0 (6K) / 61.0 (32K), FactCon-MH 80.0 / 14.0; the authors call performance 'drastically low'. §3: 'newer facts have larger serial numbers'; built from 'counterfactual edit pairs from MQUAKE'.

points.point: EvoMemBench reruns FactConsolidation on 15 memory methods: no memory method exceeds 7% on multi-hop, and a long-context model reaches 96 on single-hop against at most 54 for memory methods, so retention is far ahead of revision.
points.paper: llm/memory/benchmarks/EvoMemBench. Benchmarking Agent Memory from a Self-Evolving Perspective.md
points.evidence: Table 3, §5.2.1 (p. 6): FC MH is 7.00 for BM25 and Mem0, 5.00 for A-MEM, 3.00 for MemOS, 2.00 for MemoryOS; FC SH is 96.00 for Gemini-3-Flash, 54.00 for BM25, 49.00 for Mem0. Finding 2: 'Existing memory methods are better at retention than revision.' Long-context LLMs themselves score 58, 24 and 10 on FC MH.

points.point: In HaluMem, most memory systems have update omission rates above 50%, mainly because the pre-update memory was never extracted, so the update cannot be processed.
points.paper: llm/memory/benchmarks/HaluMem. Evaluating Hallucinations in Memory Systems of Agents.md
points.evidence: §6.2.1 (p. 11): 'most systems suffer omission rates above 50%. This issue primarily stems from insufficient coverage in memory extraction: when the pre-update memories are not extracted, related updates cannot be properly processed.' Two answers misstate it: one says the new fact was never extracted, another says 'more than half of failed updates fail because…'; the paper says the omission rate itself exceeds 50%, and the cause is the pre-update memory.

points.point: ForgetEval: deterministic stores pass 63–68% of the 385 adversarial forgetting cases (about 70% excluding compound_fact), and one LLM call at mutation time lifts this to about 92–93% (93–94% excluding compound_fact).
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting. An Architectural Study of Agent Memory Across Thirteen.md
points.evidence: Table 2, §5.3 (p. 6): Lethe 63.4, Mem0 68.3, LangMem 62.9, Lethe+LLM 91.7 on the full 385; 70.7 / 76.2 / 70.1 → 93.3 excluding compound_fact. Abstract: 'deterministic 70.1–70.7% → hook 93.3–94.2% … headline overall 91.7–93.2%'. Both the '63–68 → ~92' and '~70 → ~93' versions are correct for their denominators.

points.point: ForgetEval's main finding is that where the LLM sits matters: an LLM at write (inscribe) time hurts deletion. Mem0 with LLM inference on drops to 43.6% (68.3% without) because it links and keeps the old fact instead of deleting it; a mutation-time hook recovers intent-aware deletion.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting. An Architectural Study of Agent Memory Across Thirteen.md
points.evidence: Limitations (p. 9): infer=False '263/385 = 68.3%', 'Mem0+v3 43.6%'. §5.7 (p. 8): 'Mem0+v3's LINK-AND-KEEP collapses on deletion-precision'. Appendix P (p. 21): the router 'systematically routes "A says X" followed by "A says Y" to LINK-AND-KEEP rather than UPDATE-AND-DELETE, leaving the old fact in the store' (a 24.7-pt drop). Inscribe-time LLM does help canonicalisation categories.

points.point: In ForgetEval, graph memories do worst on targeted forgetting: Graphiti passes 7.0% and HippoRAG 9.5% of evaluable cases, because knowledge-graph abstraction discards the surface wording the tests need and Graphiti lacks purge/release primitives.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting. An Architectural Study of Agent Memory Across Thirteen.md
points.evidence: Appendix N, Table 13 (p. 19): Graphiti 17/242 evaluable (7.0%), strict 4.4%; 'Knowledge-graph abstraction sheds the surface forms our adversarial layer probes … a categorical mismatch, not a parameter-tuning issue'; no query-addressable purge or release. Limitations (p. 9): 'HippoRAG scores 31/326 evaluable (9.5%)'. These numbers are not in Table 2 on p. 6, where several answers place them.

points.point: ForgetEval shows recall quality says nothing about forgetting: a verbatim-retention store (MemPalace) passes 0 of 385 forgetting cases yet scores respectably on a recall-heavy benchmark; a case passes only if the superseded fact is absent from the top-10 recall.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting. An Architectural Study of Agent Memory Across Thirteen.md
points.evidence: §5.5, Table 3 (p. 6–7): 'MemPalace scores 0/385 on ForgetEval-Adv (forgetting-heavy) vs. 60/150 (40%) on Memora (recall-heavy) — no scalar metric captures both directions.' §3: 'A case passes iff must_contain ⊆ top-10 blob and must_not_contain ∩ top-10 blob = ∅.'

points.point: ForgetEval caveats: single author whose own store is a tested system; substring scoring, with 30% of audited failures being scorer artefacts; the hook's lift shrinks to about 12–18 points on externally authored cases; +8 points with Qwen and none with Llama; no gain on MemoryAgentBench's FactConsolidation.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting. An Architectural Study of Agent Memory Across Thirteen.md
points.evidence: Frontmatter: one author (Dongxu Yang). Appendix U (p. 25): '35/50 true failures, 15/50 scorer artifacts'. Appendix R (p. 22): hook lift '+11.7 Lethe, +18.1 LangGraph … attenuated relative to in-house (+28–30)'. Limitations (p. 9): Qwen-2.5-72B 'a smaller +8-pt lift', Llama-3.1-70B 'fails to parse our prompt contract, falling through to the deterministic baseline'. Appendix J (p. 17): hook variants score 'identically' on FactConsolidation. On the same external subset the joint Letta+LLM lift grows to +27.8.

points.point: DynamicMem: no architecture both retains stable facts and overwrites changed ones. All systems handle a fresh preference change (70–89%), but as history grows merging systems collapse (A-Mem 89% → 39%, SimpleMem 89% → 47%) while append-only ones hold better (HippoRAG2 88% → 63%, RAG 85% → 59%); the authors attribute this to merging blurring the old/new boundary.
points.paper: llm/memory/benchmarks/DynamicMem. A Long-Horizon Memory Benchmark in Real-World Settings.md
points.evidence: Finding 3 (p. 10): 'Retention and update are separate failure modes. No single architecture wins on both'; 'All systems handle a fresh preference change well at C2 (70–89%), but … A-Mem (89% → 39%) and SimpleMem (89% → 47%) decline sharply, while HippoRAG2 (88% → 63%) and RAG (85% → 59%)…'; merge-based approaches 'blur the boundary between new and old as more content accumulates'.

points.point: MemSyco-Bench: retrieving both versions is the dangerous case. A-Mem retrieves old and updated memories together in 98.6% of update cases yet scores about 24%; Mem0 scores 53.06 when only the updated memory is retrieved and 26.38 when both appear. External memory often raises outdated-memory use over full dialogue (16.3% to 41–49% with Mem0 and LightMem).
points.paper: llm/memory/benchmarks/MemSyco-Bench. Benchmarking Sycophancy in Agent Memory.md
points.evidence: Obs. 9: 'A-Mem retrieves both old and updated memories in 98.57% of cases, but still reaches only 24.06 Acc … Mem0 … Acc is 53.06 when only the updated memory is retrieved, but falls to 26.38 when old and updated memories appear together.' Obs. 3: 'for DeepSeek-V4-Flash from 16.34 to 41.42 with Mem0 and 48.57 with LightMem'. The 16→41–49 figure is for one backbone; for Qwen3-8B the baseline is 56.16.

points.point: A system can know the update and still act on the old value: the Stale benchmark's write-side prototype resolves the user's current state 91% of the time but adapts open-ended behaviour only 32% of the time, with the updated evidence visible in 67.8% of the failed cases.
points.paper: llm/personalization/methods/When Memory Updates but Behavior Does Not. Repairing Implicit Stale Dependencies in Personalized.md
points.evidence: §1 (p. 1): 'The benchmark's write-side prototype achieves 91% accuracy on state resolution but only 32% on IPA, and the updated evidence is visible in 67.8% of failed IPA cases.' This is reported second-hand from the Stale benchmark (Chao et al. 2026), which is not in the library.

points.point: StateAuditor audits from stored state to draft (the stale dependency is usually unsaid) and repairs only on verified old→new transitions, gaining 5 points on Stale (.686 → .736). Limits: no gain on a harder authored set, and a weaker auditor over-corrects (LongMemEval knowledge-update .816 → .579).
points.paper: llm/personalization/methods/When Memory Updates but Behavior Does Not. Repairing Implicit Stale Dependencies in Personalized.md
points.evidence: Abstract and §6.1 (p. 5): 'strict single-query VTA scores .736 against .686 … a +5.0-point paired gain'. §6.4 (p. 7): 'the mid-capability auditor (gpt-4o-mini) sharply lowers conflict-free accuracy (LongMemEval knowledge-update .816 → .579)'. Limitations: the harder 120-scenario set gives 'no accuracy gain'.

points.point: HorizonBench: with the full history in context and no memory system, the best of 25 frontier models reaches 52.8%; all 25 do worse on evolved than static preferences and pick the pre-change value on over a third of wrong answers (25% by chance). The changes are implied by life events, not restated, so 'most recent statement wins' returns the stale value.
points.paper: llm/personalization/benchmarks/HorizonBench. Long-Horizon Personalization with Evolving Preferences.md
points.evidence: §1 and §6.1 (p. 7): 'the best of 25 frontier models (Claude-opus-4.5) achieves 52.8%'. §6.2 (p. 8): 'selecting the outdated value on over a third of wrong answers, approximately 1.5× the uniform baseline'; 'All 25 models perform worse on evolved preferences than static ones (−2.7 pp average)'. §4: 'retrieving the most recently expressed value yields an outdated answer'. Human majority-vote accuracy is only 56–64%.

points.point: In HorizonBench, shortening the history to about 95K tokens makes anchoring worse (47.7% of errors pick the outdated value), so the failure is belief revision, not finding the evidence.
points.paper: llm/personalization/benchmarks/HorizonBench. Long-Horizon Personalization with Evolving Preferences.md
points.evidence: §6.3, Table 2 (p. 8): short-horizon variant ('0–14 day recall window, ~95K tokens') has Dist.% 47.7 against 38.2 for the neutral condition, and Evo Δ −5.7 pp (25/25 models). 47.7% is the share of wrong answers on evolved items that pick the pre-evolution distractor, not the share of all answers.

points.point: Model editing is the parametric version of the problem and is really belief revision (12 open problems). In a controlled testbed (one 83M-parameter model, one editor) the edited fact itself succeeds, but accuracy on downstream facts that should change falls from 0.97 to 0.01.
points.paper: llm/memory/parametric/Fundamental Problems With Model Editing. How Should Rational Belief Revision Work in LLMs.md
points.evidence: Abstract: 'model editing is essentially belief revision … 12 open problems'. Table 4 (§6.4–6.5, p. 13–14), 'Edit Requests w/ Downstream Answer Changes': s1 r1 generative accuracy 0.90 → 1.00, s1 r2 (downstream) 0.97 → 0.01. §6.5: 'model edits totally fail to generalize to downstream probabilistic consequences, achieving just 1% accuracy'. §6.3: 'an 83m parameter autoregressive Transformer'.

points.point: Parametric memory pools forget by age, not by obsolescence: MemoryLLM randomly drops memory tokens at each update, so older knowledge decays exponentially whether or not it has been superseded.
points.paper: llm/memory/parametric/MEMORYLLM. Towards Self-Updatable Large Language Models.md
points.evidence: §3.1 (p. 2–3), Figure 1: 'We randomly drop K tokens in θ_l'; 'knowledge within the memory pool would be exponentially forgotten at a rate of K/N', inspired by the Ebbinghaus curve. That this ignores whether a fact was superseded is the answers' inference; the paper itself calls it forgetting 'stale knowledge'.

points.point: PersonaMem-v3: Mem0 with RAG gives an outdated stance in 51.4% of preference-change cases, against 25.7% for a self-rewritten textual memory.
points.paper: llm/personalization/benchmarks/PersonaMem-v3. Toward Omni-Platform Personal Intelligence for Holistic User Understanding.md
points.evidence: Tracking-preference-changes probe: 'GPT-5.5 Textual Memory performs best … 79.9% with a 25.7% outdated rate … Mem0 with RAG is weakest, at 56.9% with a 51.4% outdated-stance rate, showing that a topically relevant retrieved fact can remain too sticky after expiry.' I did not check the page number (p. 17) the answers cite.

points.point: Other non-destructive designs: Memanto flags a contradiction and asks the agent to supersede, retain or annotate, keeping superseded entries (untested on contradictions); Belief Memory keeps competing candidates with Noisy-OR probabilities, cuts a contradicted one to 0.25, archives the old version and down-weights stale entries at retrieval.
points.paper: llm/memory/agent/Memanto. Typed Semantic Memory with Information-Theoretic Retrieval for Long-Horizon Agents.md
points.evidence: Memanto: 'three resolution options: supersede (replace the old memory), retain (keep the old memory), or annotate'; 'Memory supersession is non-destructive: superseded entries are marked accordingly but retained'; 'neither LongMemEval nor LoCoMo systematically tests contradictory memories'. Belief Memory (llm/memory/agent/Belief Memory. Agent Memory Under Partial Observability.md, §3): 'BeliefMem archives the old version … if the observation supports a competing candidate for the same attribute c, its probability would be reduced to 0.25'; 'an entry's retrieval priority decays with staleness'.

nonotes-q1-r1.comment: Every number and page I checked matches the papers: A-TMA 0.812/0.425/0.725 is correctly scoped to one profile, Zep 76.9→74.4 is on p. 7, ForgetEval 63–68% → ~92% is Table 2 on p. 6, the 30% scorer-artefact audit, no hook gain on FactConsolidation, HaluMem p. 11, HorizonBench p. 1, model editing 1% in §6.5 on p. 13. The 12-system count and the library-gap claims (Stale, Memora, MQuAKE, MemConflict not held) are correct. Points 2, 8, 20 and 30 are stated only in part (no three levels, no s=10 or graph variant, Memanto without Belief Memory). It leaves out the full-LTP figures, EvoMemBench, DynamicMem, MemSyco-Bench and PersonaMem-v3.

errors.quote: Zep is the best system on knowledge updates in the independent comparison, but at 155 s per query ([Are We Ready, p. 9, Table 2]
errors.paper_says: Table 2 (§4.3, p. 9) has no latency. The 155.1 s is in §4.5 / Figure 11 (p. 10) and is 'Avg. Operation Latency/Query', defined as memory construction time plus query time amortised per query, not query time.

errors.quote: Mem0 with inference on drops to 43.6% on ForgetEval's adversarial cases ([p. 8]
errors.paper_says: The 43.6% (168/385, infer=True) is in Limitations (p. 9) and Appendix P (p. 20). §5.7 on p. 8 gives only the qualitative LINK-AND-KEEP explanation. Minor page error.

errors.quote: Insert only while online, reconcile in a "sleep" pass, on the argument that online updates wrongly delete non-conflicting facts ([p. 5]
errors.paper_says: §3.3 (p. 5) describes the soft-update mechanism and motivates it by latency. The argument that an LLM may misread related facts as a conflict and delete the older entry is in §5.6 'Why Soft Updates Work' (p. 9). Minor page error.

errors.quote: HaluMem and "Are We Ready" share authors with MemOS, which wins
errors.paper_says: The shared authors are real (Zhiyu Li, Feiyu Xiong), and MemOS is best overall in HaluMem. In Are We Ready MemOS does not win: O1 and O4 say no single system dominates, and on knowledge update MemOS scores 28.9 against Zep 44.4, Cognee 37.8, MemoryOS 35.6 and MemTree 31.1 (Table 2, p. 9). It leads only LoCoMo EM and the backbone ablation.

noreviews-q1-r3.comment: Broadest coverage of the benchmark evidence, including MemSyco-Bench 53.06/26.38, DynamicMem, EvoMemBench and PersonaMem-v3, all correct. The LightMem claim that the offline pass sometimes lowers accuracy holds (Table 2: 67.78→65.39, 68.64→67.07), as does Mem-α excluding conflict resolution as too synthetic. The errors are citation slips and one overstatement about MemOS. It never names ghost memory, and Memory-R1 appears without the reason for RL. It says six papers were read in part, which is a partial-reading disclosure and not reliance on a review.

errors.quote: On multi-hop conflict tests every memory system scores in single digits.
errors.paper_says: True only for EvoMemBench (memory methods ≤7% on FC-MH, Table 3, p. 6). MemoryAgentBench's multi-hop ceiling is 28% (§4.2, p. 8), which the answer itself gives later.

errors.quote: an LLM at write time makes Mem0 worse (43.6% against 68.3% without it), because it links and keeps instead of deleting. An LLM hook at mutation time reaches about 92% ([p. 6, Table 2]
errors.paper_says: Table 2 (p. 6) has 68.3% and 91.7% but not 43.6%, which is in Limitations (p. 9) and Appendix P (p. 20). Minor page error.

errors.quote: Online inserts only; updates run later, on the argument that online updates wrongly delete non-conflicting facts ([p. 5]
errors.paper_says: The mechanism is in §3.3 (p. 5), but the argument is in §5.6 (p. 9). The answer admits this point came from a digest. Minor page error.

noreviews-q1@run1.review_only: LightMem's update argument is from the existing digest, not the paper.
noreviews-q1@run1.comment: Most complete answer: it covers the mechanisms, the benchmark evidence, downstream behaviour, parametric memory and caveats, with correct numbers (EvoMemBench 96 vs 54, ForgetEval 43.6 vs 68.3, A-TMA 0.812/0.425/0.725, StateAuditor .686→.736). User as Code p. 10, Belief Memory p. 12 and A-TMA p. 20 check out. The single-digits line in the summary overgeneralises but is corrected in the body. It says seven papers lack notes and then lists six, which I could not check against the papers. Points 16 and 19 are made only in part.

errors.quote: In ForgetEval, graph memories pass 7–9.5% of adversarial deletion cases and Mem0 with LLM inference 43.6%. One LLM call at the moment of change lifts plain stores from 63–68% to about 92–93% ([p. 6, Table 2]
errors.paper_says: Table 2 (p. 6) holds only the 63–68% and 91.7–93.2% figures. Graphiti's 7.0% is in Appendix N (Table 13, p. 19), HippoRAG's 9.5% and Mem0's 43.6% are in Limitations (p. 9), with Mem0's breakdown in Appendix P (p. 20). Minor page error.

errors.quote: **Label at read time.** A-TMA tags each fact as current, superseded or transitional
errors.paper_says: A-TMA is not read-time only. It works at three levels (§4.2, p. 6), and the labels are first kept in the bank (§4.3 Bank Level State Maintenance), then used for retrieval (§4.4) and QA (§4.5).

asis-q1-r2.review_only: This comes from the library's memory review and the papers it cites; I checked the figures below against the papers or their notes.
asis-q1-r2.misleading: Mildly: it has no evidence on the downstream failure (system knows the update but acts on the old value: Stale, HorizonBench, MemSyco-Bench), so the reader sees obsolete facts as only a storage and retrieval problem.
asis-q1-r2.comment: All figures given are correct (Zep 44.4 vs Mem0 15.6 / Letta 17.8 / long context 20.0, DynamicMem 89→39 and 63, A-TMA temporal F1 0.0295→0.1705 with accuracy 0.3707→0.3178, the 12–18 point external lift, 0.97→0.01 on one 83M model). It is the narrowest answer: no ghost memory, HaluMem, StateAuditor, HorizonBench, MemSyco-Bench or PersonaMem-v3. It openly says it rests on a review and on notes.

errors.quote: On A-TMA's benchmark, Graphiti retrieves supporting evidence 81% of the time but gets 42.5% conflict accuracy; adding state labels raises it to 72.5%
errors.paper_says: These are figures for one profile (LTP profile000, §1). On the full LTP benchmark (Table 2, p. 10) Graphiti/Zep has 0.711 evidence support and 0.480 conflict accuracy, rising to 0.720 with A-TMA.

errors.quote: Graphiti's 7% there is a missing-primitives mismatch, not a fair ranking.
errors.paper_says: The 7.0% (17/242) is over evaluable cases only. Cases needing primitives Graphiti lacks are marked N/A and excluded (strict denominator 4.4%). Appendix N (p. 19) attributes the low score to knowledge-graph abstraction shedding the surface forms the tests probe, 'a categorical mismatch'.

errors.quote: The critique in [Fundamental Problems With Model Editing, p. 4] is that editing is belief revision: nobody can specify which downstream beliefs should change, and there is no reason a small finetune maps to a learned revision process.
errors.paper_says: §3 (p. 4–6) covers only the first half. The argument that a few gradient steps need not amount to belief revision is §5.3 'No Learned Belief Update Mechanism' (p. 9). Minor page error.

nonotes-q1@run1.comment: Best statement of the A-TMA and Zep mechanisms (ghost memory with the address example, four timestamps, Mem0's graph variant, the Memory-R1 dog case). The ForgetEval 70% → 93% figures are the excluding-compound_fact headline, though the answer does not say so. '11-system comparison' matches Table 2's wording. Thin on benchmark numbers: no 28% or 7% on FactConsolidation, and no HaluMem, DynamicMem, MemSyco-Bench or PersonaMem-v3. 'Recall quality says nothing about forgetting' is asserted without the MemPalace evidence. The model-editing section has no testbed result.

errors.quote: In HaluMem, update omission exceeds 50% for most systems because the new fact was never extracted
errors.paper_says: HaluMem §6.2.1 (p. 11): the omissions stem from the pre-update memories not being extracted, so related updates cannot be processed. It is the old fact that is missing, not the new one.

errors.quote: LightMem's "sleep-time" pass, argued on the grounds that online updates wrongly delete non-conflicting facts ([p. 5]
errors.paper_says: That argument is in §5.6 Analysis of Sleep-Time Update (p. 9). §3.3 on p. 5 only describes the mechanism and motivates it by latency.

errors.quote: MEMIT has no deletion operation ([p. 9]
errors.paper_says: MEMIT p. 9 (§6 Discussion and Conclusion) lists limits on specificity and directional (s,r,o) relations; it says nothing about deletion, and the word does not occur in the paper.

errors.quote: (Mem0 with inference 43.6%, Graphiti 7.0%), while an LLM hook at mutation time reaches about 92% ([p. 6, Table 2]
errors.paper_says: Table 2 (p. 6) has only Lethe, Mem0 infer=False (68.3%), LangMem, MemPalace and Lethe+LLM (91.7%); the paper says Graphiti is kept out of it. The 43.6% is in Limitations (p. 9) and Appendix P, the 7.0% in Appendix N (p. 19). The paper attributes Graphiti's score to knowledge-graph abstraction and missing purge/release primitives, not to a write-time LLM.

noreviews-q1-r2.comment: Accurate on the main picture, and the claims about what the library lacks hold (Stale, MemTrace and AriadneMem are not in it). The errors are one reversed cause (HaluMem) and three wrong page or table citations. Point 9 is only half stated (Memory-R1 learns the choice, without the reason); points 16, 18 and 19 are touched but not stated. The LightMem 67.78 → 65.39 figure is correct.

errors.quote: Recording that a fact was superseded is largely solved
errors.paper_says: The library's papers say otherwise: HaluMem (p. 11) finds update omission above 50% for most systems; ForgetEval's deterministic stores pass only 63–68% of adversarial cases (p. 6, Table 2); Are We Ready (p. 9, Table 2) has Mem0, Letta and SimpleMem below plain long context on knowledge updates.

errors.quote: MEMIT can write 10,000 facts at once but has no delete operation (p. 9)
errors.paper_says: 10,000 edits is correct (pp. 7–8). Page 9 (§6) does not discuss deletion; the paper never states this.

errors.quote: (Mem0 with inference on: 43.6%), while an LLM hook at mutation time reaches about 92% on adversarial cases ([Control-Plane, p. 6, Table 2]
errors.paper_says: Table 2 on p. 6 shows Mem0 with infer=False at 68.3%; the 43.6% infer=True figure is in Limitations (p. 9) and Appendix P (p. 20).

errors.quote: contradiction resolution is the weakest ability in BEAM, at 0.05 or below for every model and method (Table 1)
errors.paper_says: The maximum in Table 1 is 0.053. More importantly, BEAM's contradiction-resolution task tests noticing that the user made two incompatible statements and asking which is correct (ideal answer, Appendix); BEAM scores Knowledge Update as a separate ability, so this number is not evidence on obsolete facts.

noreviews-q1-r1.misleading: The opening claim that recording supersession is 'largely solved' and that the only open failure is downstream contradicts the write-side evidence (HaluMem, ForgetEval, Are We Ready). A reader would wrongly conclude the storage step needs no attention. 'Most system numbers are vendor-run' also undersells the evidence: most numbers the answer itself cites come from independent benchmark papers.
noreviews-q1-r1.comment: Strongest on the retrieval and answer layers (MemSyco, HorizonBench, Stale), and the only answer to cite MemSyco's both-versions result. Checked and correct: Zep's 5.0 on MemoryAgentBench selective forgetting, HorizonBench's 56–64% human accuracy, Larimar's forget operation on p. 3. 'About 25 papers' is a little high; it cites 21.

errors.quote: BEAM's contradiction resolution is at most 0.053 for every method.
errors.paper_says: The number is right (Table 1), but it is listed under resolving changed facts across hops. BEAM's contradiction task is detecting two incompatible user statements and asking which holds; Knowledge Update is scored separately.

errors.quote: In DynamicMem, plain append-only retrieval tracks preference changes best.
errors.paper_says: DynamicMem Finding 3 (p. 10): HippoRAG2 stands out, averaging 68% against 56–59% for the other systems, plain RAG included. RAG only holds up better than the merging systems as history grows (85% → 59%).

errors.quote: raise Graphiti/Zep's temporal F1 on LoCoMo from 0.03 to 0.17 and conflict accuracy from 0.48 to 0.72
errors.paper_says: The conflict-accuracy gain is on the LTP benchmark (p. 10, Table 2), not on LoCoMo; the sentence reads as if both are LoCoMo results.

asis+claude-sonnet-5-5-q1-r1.review_only: I answered from the review and did not open the individual papers or their notes, so the numbers and what they mean are the review's, not independently checked.
asis+claude-sonnet-5-5-q1-r1.comment: Says plainly that it is unverified, and most numbers nevertheless match the papers (the Titans 27.0 → 29.0 ablation is correct: 27.01 → 29.04, Table 5, p. 16). Only one page-level citation is given for Zep and one for Are We Ready. It misses the answer-layer evidence (HorizonBench, Stale) and the HaluMem extraction point.

errors.quote: Graphiti passes 7% and HippoRAG 9.5%, and Mem0 with LLM inference 43.6%, because it links new to old instead of removing the old ([ForgetEval, p. 6, Table 2]
errors.paper_says: Only the 63–68% and 92–93% figures are in Table 2 on p. 6. The paper keeps Graphiti out of that table; Graphiti is in Appendix N (p. 19), the Mem0 infer=True figure in Limitations (p. 9) and Appendix P, HippoRAG in Fig. 2 (p. 8) and Limitations.

asis-q1-r3.review_only: MemoryBank's forgetting curve is hand-set, and the surveys list learned forgetting as open. I have this from the review only.
asis-q1-r3.comment: The most accurate answer. Its BEAM correction is right: the ideal answer in the paper is to flag the contradiction and ask which statement is correct, and Knowledge Update is a separate ability. Belief Memory (p. 12, A.2, 0.25), the o4-mini length collapse (p. 10, Table 5), HaluMem's cause and the DynamicMem numbers all check out. The claims about missing notes and the unwritable review could not be checked.

errors.quote: BEAM's best contradiction-resolution score is 0.053 (p. 8, Table 1).
errors.paper_says: The number is right, but it is given as evidence that changed facts needing a second reasoning step are unsolved. BEAM's contradiction task is noticing two incompatible user statements and asking which is correct; Knowledge Update is scored separately.

errors.quote: Nothing propagates an update to its consequences in a text store. Belief Memory is a first attempt.
errors.paper_says: Belief Memory (§3.3 p. 5, A.2 p. 12) keeps competing candidates with probabilities, cuts a contradicted one to 0.25 and archives the old version; it does not propagate an update to dependent facts. The library does hold a paper on exactly this: When Memory Updates but Behavior Does Not repairs replies that depend on a superseded state (.686 → .736 on Stale, p. 5).

asis-q1-r1.review_only: The review names Larimar as the only in-model memory here that can delete one fact exactly. Its note is a skim and I did not check the paper.
asis-q1-r1.comment: Broad and mostly accurate on the store-side evidence, and it labels its merge / unlabelled / validity-mark ranking as an inference. It omits the answer-layer papers entirely (HorizonBench, Stale, MemSyco). 'Validity-tracking stores' is a loose label for Zep and Cognee, which the paper calls graph- or relation-organised. The 70-paper count and A-TMA's July 2026 date are correct.

errors.quote: Mem0 with LLM inference on falls to 43.6% overall, because it prefers to link and keep the old fact over deleting it (p. 8).
errors.paper_says: Minor page error. The 43.6% figure (168/385, infer=True) is in the Limitations section on p. 9 and in Appendix P on p. 20. §5.7 on p. 8 only says Mem0+v3's link-and-keep collapses on deletion precision, with no overall figure in its text.

errors.quote: The 2026 papers (A-TMA, ForgetEval, HorizonBench) say it spans three levels, and a single QA score hides which one failed: bank maintenance, retrieval, answer-time resolution
errors.paper_says: Only A-TMA makes the bank / retrieval / QA split (p. 1 Introduction, §4.2 on p. 6). ForgetEval's axis is where the LLM sits in the pipeline (inscribe time, mutation time or none; §5.7, p. 8). HorizonBench tests 25 models with the full history in context and has no memory layers at all (§6, p. 7–8).

noreviews+claude-sonnet-5-5-q1-r1.review_only: I've been reading the library's memory folders and paper notes ... I only read the abstract and introduction of A-TMA, DynamicMem and Belief Memory, because they have no notes yet.
noreviews+claude-sonnet-5-5-q1-r1.comment: Broadest correct coverage, and its numbers check out (Mem0 s=10, Zep invalidation, A-TMA 0.812/0.425 and +0.24, ForgetEval 43.6 / 7.0 / 9.5 / 63–68 → 92, MemoryAgentBench 100/80 → 61/14, Are We Ready 44.4 / 15.6 / 17.8 / 6.7 / 20.0, editing 0.97 → 0.01, survey p. 59). Point 7 is not counted: it gives only Zep's favourable gpt-4o row (78.2 → 83.3) and omits the gpt-4o-mini drop (76.9 → 74.4), though it does flag the result as vendor-run. Point 19 is not counted: it states the top-10 absence criterion but not the 0/385 recall-versus-forgetting contrast. The 0.812/0.425 pair is from LTP profile000, which the answer does not say. The model-editing figures cited to p. 14 sit in Table 4 under §6.4–6.5 (heading p. 13), within the section's range. I could not check the claims that Mem0's LoCoMo category labels are permuted or that MemoryBank has no forgetting ablation.

errors.quote: More than half of failed updates fail because the original fact was never extracted
errors.paper_says: HaluMem §6.2.1 (p. 11): "most systems suffer omission rates above 50%. This issue primarily stems from insufficient coverage in memory extraction". The 50% is the share of required updates that are omitted, not the share of failed updates caused by missing extraction; the paper does not quantify the cause.

errors.quote: the gain shrinks to 12–18 points on cases from other benchmarks
errors.paper_says: The +11.7 / +18.1 pt lift is on a 77-case external-authored subset of ForgetEval, written by four blind contributors (abstract p. 1; Appendix R, p. 21–22). These are not cases from other benchmarks. On the one other forgetting benchmark the reference notes, there is no gain.

errors.quote: Merging memories to stay current destroys what was still true. In DynamicMem, A-Mem falls from 89% to 39%
errors.paper_says: The 89% → 39% drop is on the update probe (facts that have changed), not on retention of facts that stayed true (Finding 3, p. 10). On habit retention A-Mem does not decay and ends 5.7 points above C2. The paper attributes the update drop to merging blurring the old/new boundary. The answer also files this under "The update is never stored", which is not what the result shows.

errors.quote: Shortening the history to about 95K tokens makes it worse (47.7% outdated answers)
errors.paper_says: Minor. 47.7% is the distractor rate: the share of wrong answers on evolved preferences that pick the pre-change value (§6.3, Table 2, p. 8). It is not 47.7% of all answers.

errors.quote: Every result rests on its own synthetic benchmark, so the numbers above do not compare across papers.
errors.paper_says: False for results the answer itself cites. Are We Ready is an independent comparison on LongMemEval's knowledge-update slice (§4.3, p. 9), and the answer calls it "an independent test". EvoMemBench reruns MemoryAgentBench's FactConsolidation (§5.2.1, p. 6). StateAuditor is scored on the third-party Stale benchmark.

asis-q1@run1.review_only: This comes from the library's two reviews (`reviews/llm/memory.md`, `reviews/llm/personalization.md`); I did not reopen the papers, and several of them (A-TMA, Belief Memory, BEAM, DynamicMem, Larimar) were only skimmed for those reviews.
asis-q1@run1.misleading: Mildly. Section 2 gives a wrong mechanism for two results (HaluMem's 50% and DynamicMem's 89 → 39), and the closing bullet says no numbers are comparable although some are independent re-runs. The headline picture — no approach is reliable, and behaviour lags the stored update — is still right.
asis-q1@run1.comment: Widest coverage and the best table and page citations: A-TMA Tables 2 and 3, Are We Ready Table 2, EvoMemBench Table 3, BEAM 0.053, ForgetEval Table 2, HorizonBench Table 2, StateAuditor Table 1, Larimar Table 4, PersonaMem-v3 p. 17 all check out. It is also the only answer with points 14, 26 and 29. But it openly rests on reviews, and it has the most misreadings. Point 15 is not counted because the HaluMem number is misstated; point 8 is not counted because it gives only the ten-nearest check, not the LLM's ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP choice. I could not check the DeMem and MEMIT claims in detail.

errors.quote: one store does respectably on recall and passes 0 of 385 forgetting cases. One LLM call at update time lifts pass rates from about 70% to about 93% ([ForgetEval, p. 8](...dest=subsection.5.7&page=8))
errors.paper_says: Minor page error. MemPalace's 0/385 against 60/150 on Memora is in §5.3 and §5.5 (p. 6, Tables 2–3). The 70.1–70.7% → 93.3–94.2% lift (excluding compound_fact) is in the abstract (p. 1), §5.3 (p. 6) and Limitations (p. 9). §5.7 on p. 8 covers the placement regimes and contains neither figure.

nonotes-q1-r2.comment: Compact and accurate; every number checked matches (A-TMA 81% / 42.5% on one profile and 0.48 → 0.72 on full LTP, MemoryAgentBench 28%, HaluMem, 44.4, 91% / 32%, 12 open problems, MemoryLLM §3.1.3 p. 3, ablation on p. 20, ForgetEval caveats on p. 9). It is the only answer besides D with the forget-by-age point, and the only one with the 0/385 recall-versus-forgetting contrast. Point 9 is not counted: it says Memory-R1 trains the choice with RL but not why. Point 10 is not counted: it gives Zep's 44.4 but not that the other systems fall below long context. The claim that Stale and Memora are not in the library is correct. It omits the personalization benchmarks (HorizonBench, DynamicMem) and the Mem0-versus-placement finding.

errors.quote: The 2026 results (A-TMA, ForgetEval, StateAuditor) are preprints evaluated largely on benchmarks their authors built.
errors.paper_says: Wrong for StateAuditor. Its headline result is on Stale, a benchmark by Chao et al. 2026 (other authors; StateAuditor is by Sun and He), reproduced by "the benchmark's disjoint judge" (p. 1, §5 Benchmarks p. 4). It also uses LongMemEval and other external sets. The answer's own last line says Stale is by Chao et al.

nonotes-q1-r3.comment: Accurate and well organised around three failure stages; every number and page checked holds (A-TMA 81% / 42.5% → 72.5% on a subset, p. 12 conclusion for mixed LoCoMo, Memory-R1 Figure 1, DynamicMem p. 1, HorizonBench 52.8% on p. 2, Are We Ready Finding 3, ForgetEval 63–68 → ~92 on p. 8–9 and 'four systems', Hase §5.3 p. 9, MemoryLLM §3.1). It is the only answer that explains why Memory-R1 trains the update choice. Point 3 is not counted because it gives only the profile-subset numbers, not the full-LTP 0.480 → 0.720. Point 17 is not counted: it says where the LLM sits matters but not that a write-time LLM hurts deletion. The claim that Stale is not in the library is correct.
